lesson.title: Enzymes: Protein Catalysts That Make Life's Chemistry Possible
lesson.summary: Enzymes are proteins, shaped by their tertiary structure, that speed up specific biochemical reactions by many orders of magnitude without being consumed or changing the reaction's overall energetics.
lesson.body:
An enzyme is a biological catalyst, overwhelmingly built from protein, that dramatically increases the rate of a specific chemical reaction without being permanently altered or used up in the process. Most named enzymes end in the suffix ase, hinting at their target, such as amylase acting on amylose starch or lactase acting on lactose. Cells rely on enzymes for nearly everything they do chemically, because without them the reactions that build and break down biological molecules would occur far too slowly at normal body temperatures to sustain a living organism. A handful of enzymes are actually made of RNA rather than protein, called ribozymes, but the vast majority of catalytic work in cells is carried out by folded protein chains.

It is important to be precise about what an enzyme changes and what it does not change. Enzymes have no effect on the overall free energy difference between reactants and products, so they cannot make an endergonic reaction spontaneous, and they do not shift the position of a chemical equilibrium. What they change is the rate at which equilibrium is reached, typically by factors of a million or more compared to the uncatalyzed reaction. That distinction matters: an enzyme is a matchmaker for a reaction that is already thermodynamically possible, not a source of extra energy.

An enzyme's catalytic power comes directly from its tertiary structure, the specific three dimensional shape a polypeptide chain adopts once it folds. As the chain folds, amino acid side chains that may be far apart in the linear sequence get pulled close together in space through hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, hydrophobic packing, and occasionally disulfide bridges. This folding creates precisely shaped pockets and grooves on the enzyme's surface, and one of these pockets typically becomes the active site, the region responsible for binding a particular molecule and carrying out chemistry on it. Because the shape and chemical environment of this pocket are so specific, most enzymes act on only one substrate or a small family of closely related substrates, a property called specificity.

Catalase offers a vivid illustration of just how effective this machinery can be. Hydrogen peroxide, a toxic byproduct generated during normal cellular metabolism, breaks down into water and oxygen extremely slowly on its own, but catalase, found in peroxisomes, accelerates this decomposition to one of the fastest rates known for any enzyme, protecting cells from oxidative damage. A single catalase molecule can process an enormous number of hydrogen peroxide molecules every second, which underscores how thoroughly enzymes can transform a sluggish reaction into a rapid, life sustaining one.

Because enzymes emerge from protein folding, everything that shapes proteins also shapes enzyme function: temperature, pH, and any factor that disrupts the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions holding tertiary structure together can denature an enzyme and destroy its activity, since even small distortions of the active site's shape can prevent proper substrate binding. This tight link between structure and function sets up the next several ideas, including exactly how the active site is built and how the enzyme and its substrate interact once binding occurs.
